L9.6: Kidney diagram labeled Cortex, Medulla, Nephron, Renal artery, Renal vein, Ureter.
L9.7: Nephron diagram: Bowman's capsule, Glomerulus, Proximal tubule, Distal tubule, Loop of Henle, Collecting tubule. Glucose and amino acids leave the proximal tubule. Na+ and H2O leave the proximal tubule and the distal tubule. Aldosterone acts at the distal tubule and collecting tubule. ADH acts at the collecting tubule. Na+ and H2O move in the loop of Henle.
L9.12: Thick ascending limb cell diagram. Lumen urine side: Na+, K+ and 2Cl- enter together through one carrier. K+ leaks back to the lumen through a channel, giving a positive potential that drives Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption. Interstitium blood side: Na+/K+ ATPase pump, K+ and Cl- leave.
L9.21: Distal convoluted tubule cell diagram. Lumen urine side: Na+ and Cl- enter together through one transporter; Ca2+ enters through a channel. Interstitium blood side: Na+/K+ ATPase pump, Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, PTH receptor.
L9.30: Collecting tubule diagram. Principal cell: Na+ enters through a luminal channel, K+ leaves through a luminal channel, water enters through water channel molecules controlled by ADH receptor, aldosterone receptor, Na+/K+ ATPase pump on the interstitial side. Intercalated cell: H+ ATPase pump, HCO3- and Cl- exchange.
L9.34: Collecting tubule diagram. Principal cell: Na+ enters through a luminal channel, K+ leaves through a luminal channel, water enters through water channel molecules controlled by ADH receptor, aldosterone receptor, Na+/K+ ATPase pump on the interstitial side. Intercalated cell: H+ ATPase pump, HCO3- and Cl- exchange.
L9.41: Proximal tubule cell diagram. Lumen: HCO3- combines with H+ to form H2CO3, which carbonic anhydrase (CA) converts to CO2 + H2O. Inside the cell CO2 + H2O is converted back by carbonic anhydrase (CA) to H2CO3, giving H+ and HCO3-. Na+ enters in exchange for H+ at the luminal Na+/H+ exchanger. HCO3- leaves on the blood side. Na+/K+ ATPase pump. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block both CA enzymes (second picture).
L9.49: Heart failure cascade diagram. Heart failure leads to decreased cardiac output. Decreased cardiac output leads to increased venous volume and pressure with congestion and edema, dyspnea and orthopnea; decreased tissue perfusion with weakness and fatigue; neuroendocrine activation with sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation; heart rate increase; vasoconstriction with increased afterload; Na+ and H2O retention.
L9.61: Digoxin structure: a lactone ring, a steroid nucleus and three sugar molecules.
L9.62: Digitalis inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase. Intracellular Na+ concentration increases. This increases intracellular Ca2+ concentration by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. Fiber shortening (contraction) increases.
